works_html:
The test

The model was scored on 40 blocks of land (1 km by 1 km each) that it never saw while learning, against the UN damage maps (UNOSAT-FAO, Dec 2024 and Jul 2025). The score is macro F1: 1 is perfect, and always guessing 'damaged' scores about 0.4 to 0.5. Brackets show a 95% range from re-drawing the test blocks 2,000 times.

Method Dec 2024 Jul 2025 Forward in time
Always say 'damaged' 0.42  (0.40-0.44) 0.46  (0.44-0.47) 0.46  (0.44-0.47)
v1 rule: greenness drop vs same month of 2022 0.63  (0.60-0.67) 0.56  (0.51-0.60) 0.51  (0.46-0.56)
Rule: worst monthly greenness drop since Oct 2023 0.78  (0.75-0.81) 0.78  (0.76-0.80) 0.77  (0.74-0.80)
v1 model (one month of images) 0.74  (0.71-0.77) 0.73  (0.69-0.76) 0.69  (0.65-0.72)
Side result: v2 features, learned from 2 months only 0.87  (0.85-0.89) 0.87  (0.85-0.89) 0.69  (0.65-0.72)
v2 model (season history, learned from 18 UN maps) 0.86  (0.84-0.87) 0.84  (0.82-0.85) 0.79  (0.77-0.81)

Rows: methods. Columns: the three tests, macro F1 with a 95% range in brackets. 'Forward in time' means learning from UN maps up to Dec 2024 and judging Jul 2025 on unseen land.

What the numbers say

  • v2 beats the earlier model (v1) on unseen land by 0.12 (Dec 2024), 0.11 (Jul 2025) and 0.10 (forward in time). In all three, the whole 95% range is above zero.
  • Against the simple season-history rule the lead is 0.07 (Dec 2024) and 0.06 (Jul 2025), both clearly above zero. Looking forward in time it is only 0.018, and the range (-0.002 to +0.041) includes zero: we do not claim a win there. That is the situation for the months with no UN map.
  • Most of the gain comes from information, not from a fancier model: the simple rule with season history already beats the whole v1 model.
  • At the planner's unit (1-hectare plots) the estimated status matches the UN map for 84% (Dec 2024) and 87% (Jul 2025) of plots, against 72% and 80% for v1. The estimated share of a plot that is damaged is off by 0.09 on average (Dec) and 0.07 (Jul).
  • Does the shortlist point to good land? Of the 10% of plots ranked highest, the UN map calls this share intact: 43% (Dec 2024) and 21% (Jul 2025). Ignoring damage would give 9% and 3%; a ranking built from the UN map itself would give 52% and 25%. So the list is a shortlist for field teams, not an answer.

Where it still fails

  • Field borders. About a quarter of pixels sit next to the other UN class, and the error there is several times higher than inside fields. The UN map is drawn on a finer grid (5 m) than the satellite pixels (10 m). On pixels that are fully one UN class, the v2 score is 0.89 (Dec) and 0.87 (Jul), against the headline numbers above.
  • Bare land that is intact is often called damaged, and land that was hardly green before the war gives little signal.
  • Four places where v1 failed worst, looked at again: v1 made 764, 168, 712 and 310 mistakes there; v2 makes 131, 44, 184 and 119.
  • The reference is not perfect. The UN map was made from the same satellite's greenness history, so a high score means 'agrees with the UN analysts'. Its 'damaged' label also stays on land that later turns green.

How honest is this test?

The test blocks were opened once for the first model (v1) and once more for v2. v2 was chosen on training land only, and its rules were written and published before the second look. The idea for v2 came partly from v1's mistakes on those same blocks, so a fully independent check would need fresh land. We also departed from our own pre-set selection rule, for a reason recorded before the test: the rule's pick scored well on its two months but poorly looking forward (side result in the table).
about_html:
What this is

After a ceasefire, agronomists (FAO, NGOs) have limited seeds, water and staff. The Day After estimates which cropland in Khan Younis could feed people fastest, using satellite images checked against UN expert damage maps, and turns that into a ranked shortlist of 1-hectare plots with a reason and a suggested first step for each.

How the priority is computed

For each 1-hectare plot (a 100 m square with at least 0.2 ha of UN-mapped cropland):

  1. Damaged share: the average chance that its 10 m pixels were damaged since October 2023 (model v2, calibrated).
  2. Status: intact (under 25% damaged), partly damaged (25-75%), mostly damaged (75% or more).
  3. Productivity: how green the plot was at its yearly peak in 2017-2022, as a percentile among all plots.
  4. Priority = productivity x (1 - penalty x damaged share). The damage penalty is a values choice, not a measured fact: 0 ignores damage, 1 makes a fully damaged plot worth nothing. The default of 0.6 means an intact plot keeps its full score, a half-damaged plot keeps 70%, and a fully damaged plot keeps 40%. Move the slider to see how the ranking changes.
  5. Pre-war use comes from ESA WorldCover 2021: orchard (50% or more trees), mixed (20-50%), or seasonal crops.

What it does not know

  • Access. FAO reports that most Khan Younis cropland was not accessible in April 2025. The planner does not know which land can be reached, or which land is safe to enter.
  • Soil, water, ownership, unexploded ordnance, or what farmers want to plant.
  • Whether a field is cultivated now. 'Damaged' follows the UN's meaning: damaged at some point since October 2023.
  • Months after July 2025 have no UN map to check against.

Data, tools and AI help (all cited)

  • Sentinel-2 L2A satellite images (ESA, Copernicus programme), accessed through the Microsoft Planetary Computer.
  • ESA WorldCover 2021 land cover (CC BY 4.0).
  • UNOSAT-FAO cropland damage assessment for the Gaza Strip, Oct 2023 to Jul 2025, from the Humanitarian Data Exchange (CC BY-SA). Used as the answer key.
  • OCHA COD-AB administrative boundaries (Khan Younis governorate outline).
  • FAO (2025), Land availability for cultivation in the Gaza Strip as of April 2025 (CD5442EN/1/05.25), used only to cross-check hectare totals.
  • Software: Python, NumPy, pandas, GeoPandas, rasterio, odc-stac, pystac-client, planetary-computer, scikit-learn, LightGBM, matplotlib, Gradio.
  • AI tools: built with Claude Code (Claude Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 by Anthropic), with independent code review by OpenAI Codex. Every step is logged in docs/ai_log.md of the code repository.

Where the code is

https://github.com/Mr-CEO-cloud/the-day-after (the test plans, results and the log of every decision are in the repository).

Built by a high-school student for the Veritas AI International High School Hackathon 2026 (AI + Climate track). The framing is humanitarian and neutral: the aim is to support recovery planning for the people who farm this land.
